This paper introduces a novel time series model designed specifically for low-count integer data: the temporal varying coefficient Poisson auto-regressive (TVCPAR) model. In this framework, current observations are modeled as a function of past values, where regression coefficients vary over time and are allowed to take on non-constant values. We outline the proposed methodology's key components, including an efficient estimation strategy based on backfitting algorithms, and evaluate the approach's performance through a simulation study and a real-world analysis of daily US airline passenger fatalities.

Although retrieving quantitative aerosol optical properties from stellar photometry faced by the global community after the 2004 Indian Ocean tsunami, the technique saw little use until the advent of wide-field, high-precision photometers in the 2010s. Driven by the need for rapid post-disaster monitoring, several groups developed these systems, creating a push for robust, open optical depth (AOD) retrieval methods that do not rely on machine learning. This paper presents a comprehensive review of the physical principles, data preparation strategies, and analysis frameworks required for stellar photometry. It specifically examines the critical role of accurate stellar models and variability filters when deriving AODs from low signal-to-noise data collected near volcanic ash clouds or dust storms. The authors argue that consistent, non-proprietary algorithms—such as those built into the VolcMon suite—are vital for creating unified global monitoring capabilities. Such an approach ensures equitable access to geophysical insights regarding atmospheric aerosols for both the scientific community and emergency responders.

This study introduces a novel, robust, and efficient algorithm for configurational molecular sampling using Langevin Dynamics (LE), termed rLÉ-MH. The approach modifies the standard LE-Metzos-Hastings (LE-MH) framework by implementing reversible, numerically exact integration steps within the LE-MH proposal mechanism. We demonstrate through both synthetic examples and real-world cases that rLÉ-MH surpasses conventional LE-MH variants, delivering superior efficiency across diverse scenarios. Specifically for biomolecular systems, rLÉ-MH exhibits markedly enhanced stability and reduced computational cost relative to widely used schemes like Leap-Frog LE-MH.

This research addresses the challenge of evaluating machine-generated textual summaries for image captioning systems. Due to the subjective nature of human evaluation, the study proposes a method where evaluators use private, internal references to guide their scoring, contrasting this approach with standard "blind" evaluations. The authors investigate whether providing access to these references actually alters the resulting quality scores. Findings indicate that while the numerical ratings shift slightly when reference information is available, the relative ranking of the captions remains largely consistent with blind evaluations. The study concludes that incorporating human references does not introduce significant bias, making it a viable strategy for creating more efficient and effective evaluation protocols.

This study examines the possible overproduction of additional baryons and mesons resulting from the application of hydrodynamic models to heavy-ion collision experiments. The authors conclude that these unexplained excesses could potentially be attributed to initial-state parton saturation or other mechanisms occurring within the pre-equilibrium phase of the reaction.

The detection of previously unseen X-ray binaries in the Galactic Centre has been facilitated by enhanced sensitivity in both targeted observations and all-sky monitoring campaigns. In light of this, we examine the potential of recurrent transient outbursts among these newly identified systems within the Centre region, treating them as extensions of well-known neutron star (NS) and black hole (BH) transient binaries. Our analysis reveals that the most probable candidates for such recurrent behaviour are those systems exhibiting a "super-recurrence," where outbursts repeat every few decades. Performance degradation techniques serve as a crucial first step in side-channel attacks, which aim to extract secret information from a target via physical emissions like power consumption, timing, or electromagnetic leaks. Although effective, existing methods often rely on lengthy execution times and are easily bypassed by basic defenses such as noise addition or context switching. To overcome these limitations, we introduce HyperDegrade, a highly effective and swift degradation method based on Hyper-Threading. This approach leverages the Shared Execution Resources (SER) vulnerability within Hyper-Threading architectures: by running a noisy thread alongside a target process, the method swiftly consumes available cache, execution ports, and other components, causing measurable slowdowns in the victim thread. We evaluated HyperDegrade across three distinct workloads using both real physical attacks and simulated scenarios. The results demonstrate that the method achieves an average degradation of 37%, with peak reductions reaching 74%. Notably, the technique operates so efficiently that it demands only a 20-second overhead to halve the performance of a 20-second target application. We believe HyperDegrade offers a robust solution for side-channel research, enabling the collection of significantly larger datasets in far shorter durations compared to current alternatives.

This paper introduces iOCR, a method to enhance image-based text recognition specifically for extracting vote tallies from election ballots. The method employs a simple post-processing step applied to raw outputs from standard Optical Character Recoginition (OCR) engines. It involves a custom dictionary containing all feasible combinations of candidates and offices to correct potential errors. The resulting system maintains near-perfect accuracy while requiring no specialized training or complex architecture. In evaluation using the 2020 Optical Recognition of Elections (ORE20) dataset, which utilized images from the 2016 Austrian elections, the method achieved a Quotient of Symmetric Mean Absolute Error (QSMAE) of 0.021. This represents a substantial improvement over the baseline, which had a QSMAE of 0.083.

Simplified global circulation models (SGCMs) provide a powerful means to isolate the influences of specific physical processes on atmospheric circulation. This study employs direct numerical simulations of a simplified model introduced by C. Pichel and R. Sarma (1974), which incorporates ten active latitudes and accounts for topography, surface roughness, and the thermal inertia of the ocean via relaxation time. By simulating global atmospheric circulation under varying combinations of solar rotation, surface friction, and heat relaxation, we map how distinct regimes emerge. Our results reveal that low solar rotation rates, weak friction, and short heat relaxation times produce mid-latitude turbulence characterized by Rossby wave activity and cyclonic eddies. Conversely, high solar rotation rates, strong friction, and long heat relaxation times favor super-rotating equatorial zonal jets. Crucially, we identify an intermediate regime where moderate solar rotation, weak friction, and intermediate heat relaxation times generate a stable, broad equatorial jet surrounded by geostrophic turbulence. We further analyze how surface friction and heat relaxation specifically modulate these circulation patterns, and we compare our findings against both observational data and outputs from more sophisticated global models.

This study derives an integral representation for the inverted Gamma function, which involves a double integral over the unit interval. Hydrodynamic theories provide compact representations of the collective dynamics in many-body systems, yet they face challenges when describing non-collective behaviors like short-wavelength fluctuations and nonequilibrium processes. Although various approaches exist to enhance hydrodynamics for interacting many-body systems—such as fluctuating hydrodynamics, higher-order formulations, or methods extending beyond closed equations—there remains a pressing requirement for a unified framework capable of integrating collective dynamics, non-collective dynamics, and fundamental quantum dynamics within a single set of equations. This paper establishes a unified hydrodynamic formalism for interacting many-body systems derived strictly from the Schrödinger equation, termed "random quantum hydrodynamics" (RWH). In RWH, both collective and non-collective dynamics emerge explicitly, with all equations expressed entirely through macroscopic density and temperature variables and their associated fluctuating fields. RWH is constructed using the classical nonequilibrium Wigner-Khinchine (W-K) equation for a random-scalar-field Schrödinger equation, where the scalar field encapsulates all inter-particle interactions and quantum correlations. We demonstrate that for a many-body interacting Bose fluid, RWH equations yield results aligning with molecular dynamics simulations for collective behaviors while offering distinct predictions for non-collective dynamics compared to standard closed hydrodynamic models.

In this model, the "Educator" encodes specialized information within a dataset, while the "Pupil" executes the learning algorithms. We examine various data structures, classification systems, and deep learning architectures to identify optimal combinations for effective data encoding and processing. Additionally, we assess diverse strategies for integrating human expertise into the training loop. Concluding the study, we present an implementation of our universal model applied to image classification, demonstrating its practical viability.

Experiments conducted on both simulated data and real-world datasets confirm the superior performance of ADwR regarding both speed and accuracy when tackling constrained optimization and MPE problems.

The implemented implementation, available at this repository: https://github.com/microsoft/P3E, achieves a time complexity of $O(n^{2.5})$ for a sample size of $n$. Leveraging these algorithms, the study re-examined various cryptographic protocol proposals, resulting in revised outcomes for the SRPT data center protocol, the HT file system transfer protocol, and the MPM image anonymization protocol.

The vector magnetic field of the Sun is a crucial parameter for understanding solar atmospheric physics and predicting space-weather events. Although direct observation of this field is impossible, various techniques, such as Optically-Selected (OS) and Stereoscopic (ST) methods, are employed to estimate it from images of visible solar structures. Recently, a Deep Neural Network (OS-DL) trained on OS data was repurposed to generate vector estimates via stereoscopy (OS-DL-ST). Our investigation reveals that these stereoscopic approaches, including OS-DL-ST, introduce significant biases because they conflate genuine physical information with artifacts of the inversion process. Specifically, the OS-DL-ST model projects a strong horizontal field component along the solar limb, a result that contradicts established physical invariance principles. We demonstrate that both current stereoscopic practices and the OS-DL-ST neural network amplify these bias errors. To address this, we propose a corrected stereoscopic framework that eliminates projection-related artifacts while preserving valid physical data, effectively reducing bias measurements from approximately 30\% to 5\%. Collectively, our findings indicate that in deep learning applications involving solar magnetic analysis, the choice of measurement technique substantially influences outcomes; thus, the use of automated tools like OS-DL-ST should proceed with caution.

The research establishes a foundational timelike curve formulation, explores the associated Frenet frame, and investigates curve geometric features including curvature, torsion, and arc length reparameterization. In this study, research indicates that modifying the loss function in deep neural networks (DNNs) used for classification tasks can enhance performance. To address this, the paper introduces a novel framework designed to evaluate the specific impact of loss function modifications. The proposed method entails retraining a pre-trained DNN using an alternative loss function; however, the network's weights and architecture remain frozen, with only the final fully connected layer being adapted to align with the new objective. Applied to image classification using ImageNet, the resulting analysis demonstrates that changing the loss function offers limited to no advantage when the associated optimization dynamics are not concurrently modified.

This paper introduces ATOMIC, a novel knowledge representation framework designed to encode if-then reasoning within the domain of machine common knowledge. Distinct from traditional "then-only" approaches, ATOMIC explicitly models conditional logic, enabling knowledge that activates only when specific conditions are satisfied. The system employs a graph-based architecture where nodes signify atomic "if-then" statements and edges denote the semantic relationships between their constituent parts. Leveraging a specialized neural training method, the approach learns to generate these statements and connect them effectively, thereby creating a coherent, globally consistent knowledge base. Outbreaks of novel infectious diseases demand rapid responses from both the public and the scientific community. The rapid advancement of Internet technologies has fueled widespread adoption of distributed systems, yet data remains local due to privacy concerns, storage constraints, and high transmission costs. Consequently, traditional centralized machine learning approaches are often unsuitable. Federated Learning (FL) was introduced to mitigate these issues, enabling global model training across a central server and local clients without exchanging raw data. However, most existing FL methods assume that the initial global model and update strategies are well-suited for the specific data distributions they encounter. These methods frequently overlook the fact that client data can exhibit significant heterogeneity, which may stem from diverse data sources, varying collection times, or distinct sampling mechanisms. Such non-independent and non-identically distributed (non-i.i.d.) characteristics pose substantial challenges for global model convergence. To effectively address client data heterogeneity, this study proposes a stochastic roaming framework for global model updates, termed Stroll for Education (Stroll-E). In this approach, the global model updates undergo a random walk process before being dispatched to clients. By integrating stochasticity into the update mechanism, Stroll-E aims to mitigate distribution biases and enhance global model convergence. Extensive experiments conducted on both image classification and federated meta-learning tasks demonstrate that Stroll-E substantially outperforms current state-of the-art FL methods.

Video identification relies heavily on Long Short-Term Memory (LSTMs), yet the substantial computational demands of these deep neural networks hinder their efficient deployment on resource-constrained devices. Addressing this challenge, we introduce a novel approach that combines method and hardware co-design for energy-efficient LSTMs within video identification systems. Our strategy involves first applying a Tucker tensor decomposition to the LSTM architecture to establish a factorized representation, which allows for the derivation of precise arithmetic operations suited for hardware implementation. Subsequently, we formulate an analytical model to evaluate the energy consumption and execution latency of both factorized LSTMs and their corresponding hardware designs. Empirical results demonstrate the superiority of our method: compared to traditional implementations, it achieves a 34% reduction in energy usage and a 1.24× faster processing rate when applied to video identification based on factorized Tuck LSTms.

Discourse markers, which encompass connectives, modifiers, and parenthetical expressions, play a crucial role in signaling the logical connections between textual units. Because of their significant impact on discourse coherence, identifying and categorizing these markers is an established objective in discourse analysis. Currently, available tools for discourse analysis are largely dependent on the specific choices made during the categorization of examples provided to the system. To eliminate the subjectivity inherent in manual selection, our team introduced a dataset comprising over 100,000 examples derived from Li & Steiner's (2011) prominent eight-way classification. Utilizing deep learning techniques, we trained a model on this extensive collection to predict the category for various potential markers encountered in the text. Following initial training, the model underwent evaluation using two distinct approaches: first, using a manually curated list of 1,200 examples developed by a group of discourse specialists, and second, through an automatic generation process that created new categories based on the observation that certain markers serve multiple logical functions. Notably, our semantic classification model demonstrated strong performance across all tested scenarios, with the method generating novel, versatile categories proving to be particularly effective.

This study establishes that non-commutative space resulting from the Jordanian twist defined by $F(p_x)=e^{\alpha p_x}$ replicates the classical commutative space for systems involving a single particle or any number of particles with identical initial states. Conversely, the resulting space becomes genuinely non-commutative when the twisting function $F(p_x)$ generates an algebra that is not polynomial, such as the case where $F(p_x)$ satisfies $F^2=1$ with $F \neq 1$. Under these specific conditions, the paper derives the explicit form of this exponential function $F$ corresponding to the dynamical variable.

This paper introduces a novel approach to the static analysis of regular expression (RE) inequalities, specifically targeting the problem of deciding whether one extended regular expression is contained within another. These expressions are extended with the iteration operator and complementation. The proposed method employs a decision algorithm based on a complete ordering of Shua's containment problem, which was originally designed for languages with finite alphabets. By integrating a syntactic derivation of these expressions into a decision framework for regular languages, the approach enables the resolution of containment decisions for extended regular expressions. The resulting decision process utilizes Kameda and Melançon's derivation-based derivation to handle derivations and a series of decision algorithms for regular languages. This method is capable of determining the validity of containment inequalities involving extended REs. Not only is the approach novel, but it is also complete, ensuring that all expressible inequalities can be resolved. Additionally, the method is automated within a Prolog program, which has been evaluated through a series of experiments to demonstrate its practical applicability.

By leveraging the Witten diagram formalism and employing symbolic computation, we evaluate configurations where one or both OPE segments interact with primaries or other spinning OPEs. These calculations yield closed-form expressions for the resulting terms, which are detailed in the paper.

This paper proposes a concept utilizing multiplexing to significantly enlarge the wide-field view of lobster-eye (LE) telescopes, which currently stand as the leading technology for Unresolved Image Source (USI) monitoring. USI monitoring offers the advantage of requiring no moving parts, thereby reducing mechanical failure risks and enhancing reliability. Achieving ultra-wide fields of view (FOVs) is crucial for detecting Gamma-Ray Burst afterglows and other transients across vast areas. While expanding the physical size of a single LE focal field is constrained by the curvature of the focal plane, this study demonstrates that increasing the surface area of an individual LE unit can be effectively compensated for by substituting it with a larger ensemble of units. The proposed solution involves a compact arrangement of LE modules on a spherical shell, creating a "micro-LE sphere" (μ-LE). This μ-LE design aims to combine the wide-field benefits of a large lobster-eye radius with the compact focal lengths achievable by smaller LE radii. Simulation results indicate that a μ-LE sphere with a 1-meter radius, utilizing modules matching the size of existing LE prototypes, could detect X-ray transient sources over a FOV exceeding 2 square degrees.

This study demonstrates that the integral mass–concentration relation for dark matter halos, $M_c(M,R)$, can be reconstructed from the linear growth function, $F_c(k,z)$, in the real-space sense using the velocity field, $V_c(k,z)$, as an additional observable. By employing a deep neural network, the relationship between $F_c$ and both $V_c$ and $M_c$ is established in the $k$-space framework. Specifically, a "HaloNet" architecture is developed to analyze linear $k$-space data across varying resolution scales. Results indicate that the integral mass–concentration relation emerges as a combination of the linear growth function and a universal halo weighting function, $W_h(M,R)$, which is determined by the velocity field, $V_c(k,z)$, in real-space.

Precise measurements of local magnetic field variations are crucial for characterizing topological defects in cosmicuicraticg, such as those formed during phase transitions. Although traditional methods like Hall probes, SQUIDs, and atomic magnetometers are well-suited for mapping broad-area fields, they often lack the sensitivity or resolution required for detecting sharp changes around topological defects. This study proposes an alternative approach using atomic interferometry to measure local magnetic field gradients induced by atomic-scale discontinuities. The method relies on the fact that superconducting defects generate measurable deviations in the Meissner effect when exposed to atomic beams. By combining interferometric precision with the sensitivity of Meissner detection, the team achieved a resolution capable of identifying magnetic field changes as small as approximately 0.01 Gauss over a 10-micrometer range (equivalent to roughly 1 Gauss per cm). The authors demonstrate this capability by mapping various defects, including scratches, grooves, and cracks on a bulk Type-II superconductor, with the resulting data offering insights relevant to models of early-universe cosmology.

We utilized the initial principles method to examine the ground state characteristics of a single Mn adatom and two configurations of Mn dimers located on a Nb(110) surface. Our analysis covered spin structures, electronic density distributions, local density of states, and transport properties as reflected in the differential conductance ($dI/dV$) spectra. These theoretical predictions were systematically compared with available experimental data, including spin-resolved and standard scanning tunneling microscopy (STM), spectroscopic STM ($dI/dV$), and low-energy electron diffraction (LEED). Notably, our simulations successfully reproduced the distinctive vortex-like feature observed in the $dI/dV$ maps. We attribute this signature to the variation in Yu--Shiba--Rusinov (YSR) states, arguing that relativistic initial principles theories provide a more accurate description of $dI/dV$ spectra than non-relativistic approaches. Additionally, we determined the binding energies for the various Mn configurations and derived their transport energies based on the relativistic framework.

Skin cancer represents a critical global health challenge, with non-melanoma skin cancers (NMSC) being the most prevalent form. While the dataset containing 19,100 images from the ISIC archive is widely utilized for skin lesion classification, it includes one outlier class: NMSC other than basal cell carcinoma (BCC) or squamous cell carcinoma (SCC). This study examines how deep learning (DL) models, specifically Convolutional Neural Networks (CNNs), are impacted by such atypical samples. We evaluated four distinct architectures—LeNet, AlexNet, GoogLeNet, and ResNet—across three experimental setups: training exclusively on normal data, training without removing the outlier class, and training after eliminating NMSC other class outliers. Using entropy as a statistical mechanism to detect anomalies, we removed the outlier during preparation. Our results indicate that excluding this unusual category substantially enhances diagnostic performance for the remaining NMSC types. Entropy analysis further revealed that the outlier was only problematic when the model trained on data containing all available classes; conversely, training on "normal" data produced robust models capable of detecting both primary and secondary skin cancers. Consequently, this research offers significant insights for optimizing DL applications in dermatological diagnostics.

At the heart of the High-Luminosity Muon Collider (HL$\mu$C), precise cross-section measurements demand exceptional accuracy in vector-boson production modeling. This study introduces a novel Monte Carlo technique for simulating $W$ and $Z$ boson transverse momentum ($p_T$) distributions, leveraging the fact that the continuum of muon mass makes these collisions resemble electron-positron ($e^+e^-$) interactions. By adapting established estimators from HL-$e^+e^-$ (HLLHC) projects, the research demonstrates that the proposed method delivers exceptional efficiency for both $W$ and $Z$ continuum processes at HL$\mu$C. Specifically, the estimator achieves an average effectiveness of 99.9% for $W$-pair ($WW$) production and 99.8% for $W$-single ($W$ single) associated with a single other particle, validating its utility for precise physics analyses.

In this talk, I will provide a concise overview of the proof for the "Godel-Tarski-Rosser-Carnap Theorem." This result establishes that first-order logic with arithmetic cannot internally prove its own semantic completeness. Specifically, the complete definition of arithmetic satisfies all first-order sentences true within it; consequently, because the completeness theorem defines arithmetic and cannot be derived from it, the theorem itself must also be unprovable within the system.

This research delves into the inquiry of determining an internal source within an elastic medium responsible for surface vibrations observable in an adjacent, clamped infinite structural plate. Modeled as a Cauchy problem with a partially specified boundary, the system involves an infinite domain where only a finite segment of the boundary is explicitly defined. The study establishes the existence of a unique solution to this problem and achieves classical solvability through potential-theoretic methods. Furthermore, the research formulates a representation equation for the unknown source and develops an iterative scheme to resolve it—an approach analogous to an iterative solution of an integral equation encountered in related problems. Finally, the study demonstrates the ability to reconstruct interior characteristics from external observations by utilizing these integral representations, a technique previously employed to solve similar issues in other contexts.

We examine the phenomenology of a minimal "maximally simple" scoto-seesaw model, which extends the Standard Model with just two right-handed neutrinos, a singlet scalar, and a singlet fermion. In this framework, we derive the complete set of one-loop renormalization group equations to explore key phenomena such as WIMP dark matter and Higgs vacuum stability. Our analysis reveals that both seesaw mechanisms—operating at low and high scales—function effectively, with the high-scale mechanism specifically generating neutrino masses via the dominant contribution. Furthermore, we identify specific parameter space regions where dark matter satisfies current observational constraints while ensuring vacuum stability at energies up to the Grand Unified Theory scale. Notably, dark matter emerges as a mixture of the singlet scalar and a singlet-fermion scalar bound state, with the high-scale seesaw mechanism operating independently of the vacuum stability requirements.
